t: Introduction: mechanical injuries and transport trauma
n: This session begins with a review of mechanical injuries. The control questions cover the concept of injury, factors, classification and the vitality of an injury. On mechanical injuries, questions are asked on blunt objects, abrasion, bruise, bone deformation, fall from a height, and incised, stab and chop wounds. The next chapter is devoted to transport trauma. It includes automobile, motorcycle, rail, tractor and aviation trauma. One of the control questions on transport trauma asks about the importance of this knowledge in the physician's work. That is, medical care and forensic examination are interrelated.

t: Sawing wounds: dependence of shape on the saw
n: Let us look at the dependence of the shape of sawing wounds on the saw. Inside and at the edges of sawing wounds there are small particles of soft tissue and bone sawdust. The kerf is wider than the thickness of the saw blade. Attention: a circular saw rotates, whereas a blade saw moves forward and back, so the marks differ. With a circular saw, the edges of the wound are uneven, serrated and finely flapped, and on bone there is a smooth surface and arc-shaped marks. With a blade saw, the wound is linear, the edges are finely serrated, and parallel ridges and grooves are seen on bone. A blow with a saw produces small stab or stab-incised wounds.

t: Transport trauma: definition and significance
n: The definition and significance of transport trauma. Transport trauma is the totality of injuries received from the external and internal parts of a moving vehicle and from falling out of it. Since the 1960s it has become a separate part of forensic medicine, because there are particular features of the mechanism of injury and of forensic examination. Most often it is an accident. Occasionally suicide or an attempt is encountered; homicide by means of a vehicle is regarded as casuistry. Transport trauma accounts for 60–65% of deaths from mechanical injury. More than 90% of examinations concern automobile trauma.

t: Statistics of transport trauma
n: Statistics of transport trauma. According to the World Health Organization, that is, the WHO, more than 1.2 million people die each year. The number injured each year is more than 50 million. According to the World Bank's calculation, material loss amounts to 1.5–2.0% of the gross domestic product of all countries. In forensic examination, transport trauma accounts for 60–65% of deaths from mechanical injury. In the examination of living persons this share is 20–25%. Automobile trauma, in turn, accounts for more than 90% of all examinations.

t: Kinds of transport trauma
n: Kinds of transport trauma. Transport trauma is the totality of injuries received from parts of moving transport and from falling from it. Road transport includes the automobile, motorcycle, bicycle and tractor. Rail transport, as a separate kind, gives rail trauma. Air and water transport include aviation trauma and water transport trauma. Automobile trauma is the most frequent: it makes up more than 90% of examinations. A collision of different vehicles is called combined trauma, for example a collision of a motorcycle with an automobile.

t: Clothing and tasks at the stage of medical care
n: Clothing and tasks at the stage of medical care. The physician fully examines and describes the injuries, and also pays attention to the victim's clothing and footwear. On clothing and footwear there may be signs of injury and contamination that are important for investigating the event. Therefore they are removed carefully, dried indoors if necessary, placed in paper packaging and handed over to law enforcement authorities. On the basis of an analysis of examination materials, proposals and recommendations are given for measures aimed at reducing traumatism.

t: Quick question: basics of transport trauma
n: Quick question: basics of transport trauma. Question: what is transport trauma? Answer: the totality of injuries received from the external and internal parts of a moving vehicle and from falling out of it. Question: what is its share? Transport trauma accounts for 60–65% of deaths from mechanical injury, and in the examination of living persons for 20–25% of mechanical injuries. Question: which kind makes up more than 90% of examinations? Answer: automobile trauma; the other kinds are much less frequent. Attention: an injury received in a collision of different vehicles is called combined transport trauma, for example motorcycle–automobile.

t: Classification of automobile trauma (according to Matyshev)
n: The classification of automobile trauma according to Matyshev. According to the 1968 classification of Matyshev and co-authors, six kinds of automobile trauma are distinguished. The first is collision, that is, a blow by an automobile. The second is running over, that is, by the wheels of an automobile. The third is injury inside the automobile. The fourth is falling out of the automobile. The fifth is compression between the automobile and other objects. The sixth is the combined kind, when two or more kinds are observed together. Injuries are formed by the mechanisms of blow, compression, tension, friction and concussion. Each kind is observed in different variants; injuries depend both on the kind and on the variant.

t: Groups of injuries in automobile trauma
n: Groups of injuries in automobile trauma. Injuries are divided into four groups by diagnostic significance. Specific injuries correspond to the shape of a part of the automobile, for example a headlamp, a trim, a tread mark. Characteristic injuries correspond to the kind or phase, for example a bumper injury and a whiplash-type fracture. No conclusion is given on non-characteristic injuries, that is, abrasions, bruises and some wounds. Imitating injuries resemble those from another event, for example an incised wound from windscreen fragments. Attention: a characteristic injury corresponds to the kind; one cannot judge automobile trauma from a non-characteristic one. Specific injuries are also called contact injuries; from them it is sometimes possible to identify a particular automobile.

t: Characteristic injuries: signs corresponding to kind and phase
n: Characteristic injuries: signs corresponding to kind and phase. By mechanism of origin, characteristic injuries correspond to a particular kind or phase of automobile trauma. They include bumper injuries, marks of sliding and dragging, multiple rib fractures and blood-filled "pockets". In addition, "whiplash" fracture of the cervical vertebrae, compression fracture of the vertebral bodies and multiple fractures of the skull bones are considered characteristic injuries. Serious injuries of the internal organs of the chest and abdomen and multiple fractures of the sternum and pelvic bones are also characteristic. Remember: such injuries help to determine the mechanism.

t: Attention: non-characteristic and imitating injuries
n: Attention: non-characteristic and imitating injuries. Non-characteristic injuries, that is, abrasions, bruises and some wounds, have neither specific nor characteristic signs. No conclusion about automobile trauma can be made from them. Imitating injuries resemble injuries from other events. Incised or stab-incised wounds are formed from windscreen fragments. An injury from bolts protruding outward resembles a stab wound, so it can be confused with an injury from another event. Remember: finding an abrasion, bruise or wound does not by itself prove automobile trauma. Grouping injuries is needed to determine the mechanism.

t: Case analysis: group of injuries in automobile trauma
n: Case analysis: group of injuries in automobile trauma. Situation: an abrasion and a bruise corresponding to the shape of a headlamp were found on the victim's body. Question: to which group does this injury belong? Answer: it is a specific, that is, contact, injury. It is formed by the action of a particular part of the automobile, that is, a headlamp, trim or tyre tread. The shape, size and pattern correspond to the part of the automobile that was in contact. From this the kind of trauma, and sometimes the particular automobile, is determined. Another question: how would you explain the difference from the other three groups, that is, characteristic, non-characteristic and imitating? Such marks usually appear in the first phase, at impact.

t: Collision of a pedestrian with an automobile: four phases
n: Collision of a pedestrian with an automobile: four phases. In most cases, in a collision of a pedestrian with the front of an automobile, four phases are distinguished. The first phase is the blow by a part of the automobile. The second phase is the fall of the body onto the automobile. The third phase is being thrown and falling to the ground. The fourth phase is sliding on the ground. In a collision with a lorry, a van body and the side of a vehicle, and in young children, there is no second phase. At low speed there may be no fourth phase; in sliding, parallel abrasions are formed.

t: First phase: bumper injuries
n: First phase: bumper injuries. The action of the bumper usually forms a transversely located abrasion, bruise or wound. These injuries are called bumper injuries. A fracture of a leg bone depends on bumper height and speed. In a passenger car the bones of the lower leg break, in a lorry the femur. A bumper fracture is usually triangular, with its base on the side of the primary blow. If the bumper is thin and the speed is greater than 55–60 km/h, a ring fracture is also possible. Attention: the base of the triangle is on the side of the blow; do not say it the other way round. In this phase a "whiplash" fracture of the cervical vertebrae may also occur.

t: Injuries in phases 2–4 and skipped phases
n: Injuries from the second to the fourth phase, and skipped phases. In a collision with a lorry, a car with a van body and the side of an automobile, the second phase is not observed. In young children there is no second phase, because the initial blow falls above the centre of gravity. At low speed there may be no fourth phase. According to the comparative table, in the second phase the injury is on the side of the first impact, on the head and chest; the mechanism is blow and concussion. In the third phase the injury is on the side opposite to the first impact, the mechanism being impact with the ground and concussion. In the fourth phase, parallel abrasions corresponding to sliding are formed.

t: Case analysis: bumper fracture
n: Case analysis: bumper fracture. Situation: in a pedestrian who collided with a moving automobile, a fracture of the lower leg bones and a transverse abrasion on the leg were found. The fracture was established to be triangular. The side on which its base lies is taken to be the side from which the primary blow was delivered. A fracture of the lower leg bones corresponds to a passenger car. If the femur is broken, one thinks of a lorry. Question: what else can be judged from bumper injuries? Answer: the make of the automobile, the speed, the region of primary impact and the position of the pedestrian.

t: Running over by a wheel
n: Running over by a wheel. Attention: complete running over is not incomplete running over. In complete running over the wheel passes across the body, in incomplete running over it merely mounts the body. The direction of running over relative to the axis of the body may be transverse, oblique or longitudinal. Severe injuries are formed mainly by compression of the body between the wheel and the ground. Running over consists of five phases. The first phase is the wheel striking the body. The second phase is displacement with the wheel. The third phase is the wheel mounting the body. The fourth phase is the wheel leaving the body. The fifth phase is secondary displacement of the body.

t: Tread marks: positive and negative
n: Tread marks: positive and negative. In forensic practice, among specific injuries, impressions of the tyre tread are the more frequent. The marks occur on the body in the form of an injury mark, that is, a bruise and abrasion, and on clothing in the form of an overlay mark, that is, contamination. Attention: a positive mark is not a negative mark. A positive mark is produced by the raised part of the tread and gives an abrasion and a bruise. A negative mark is produced by the recessed part of the tread and gives only a bruise. An overlay mark arises from various kinds of contamination and is found on clothing mainly in this form.

t: Injuries of body regions when run over by a wheel
n: Injuries of body regions when run over by a wheel. When the head is run over, multiple fractures of the skull and facial bones occur, the brain is crushed, and the auricle may be wholly or partly detached. In the chest the ribs break on both sides along several lines; in the supine position the scapula and the spinous processes of the vertebrae also break. In the abdominal region the internal organs are damaged and displaced; in the pelvis there are multiple bone fractures; in the legs, comminuted fractures of the bones are observed. On the side from which the wheel passed off, the injury is more severe. If the speed is 20 km/h and above, the wheel "jumps off", so there may be no injury in the 4th phase.

t: Quick question: pedestrian and wheel injuries
n: Quick question: pedestrian and wheel injuries. Question: how many phases are there in a collision with a pedestrian? Answer: four, that is, the blow, the fall onto the automobile, being thrown and falling to the ground, and sliding on the ground. Question: what shape is a bumper fracture? Answer: triangular, with its base on the side of the primary blow. In a passenger car the lower leg breaks, in a lorry the thigh. Question: how do the positive and negative tread marks differ? Answer: a positive mark is an abrasion with a bruise, a negative mark is a bruise only. Attention: risk of error! In a collision with a pedestrian there are 4 phases, in running over by a wheel 5 phases; do not confuse them.

t: Injury inside the automobile: the driver
n: Injury inside the automobile: the driver. Injuries are on the front and left surfaces of the body; abrasions and bruises are formed from the parts of the left door. On striking the steering wheel, a semilunar abrasion appears on the chest and a contused wound on the chin, and a fracture of the sternum and ribs is possible. On the sole of the footwear there may be an impression of a pedal; at high speed a ring fracture of the occipital bone is possible. In the driver there are four phases of injury. In the first the leg strikes the panel. In the second the chest strikes the steering wheel. In the third the neck flexes and the head strikes. In the fourth the body and neck move backward.

t: Passengers and the seat belt
n: Passengers and the seat belt. The body of the front-seat passenger is not restrained: the injuries are more severe, and this is the most dangerous seat in the cabin. From windscreen fragments, incised wounds occur on the face. Rear-seat passengers are injured less often: from striking the back of the front seat and from concussion of the body. At high speed they may be thrown forward. With a sharp increase or decrease in speed, because of the movement of the head relative to the body, a "whiplash" fracture of the cervical vertebrae is possible. Attention: as speed rises, the belt itself becomes a damaging factor: rupture of a cervical ligament, fracture of the arch of the 2nd cervical vertebra, and in the elderly a fracture of the sternum and ribs.

t: Falling out of an automobile: three phases
n: Falling out of an automobile consists of three phases. In the first phase abrasions, bruises and sometimes contused and lacerated wounds are formed, that is, direct injuries. This phase is called striking parts of the automobile. The main injuries arise in the second phase and depend on which part of the body lands on the ground. In a fall onto the head, the bones of the skull and face break; onto the chest, the ribs; onto the buttocks, the pelvis. In the third phase the body slides along the ground by inertia. That is, the sequence is as follows: the blow, the body falling to the ground, then sliding on the ground.

t: Difference between falling out and falling; compression
n: The difference between falling out and falling; compression. In the third phase the body slides along the ground by inertia, and parallel band-like abrasions are formed. Falling out of a moving automobile differs from falling from a height precisely by the presence of injuries of this phase. Attention: risk of error! Falling out of an automobile is not a fall from a height, although in both there are direct and indirect injuries. In compression between parts of the automobile and other objects there are two phases: in the first a blow by external parts, in the second compression of the body.

t: Case analysis: injury inside the automobile
n: Case analysis: injury inside the automobile. Situation: after a crash, a semilunar abrasion and a bruise were found on the chest and a contused wound on the chin. Such signs correspond to a blow against the steering wheel, so the victim was probably the driver. In the driver, injuries are on the front and left surface of the body; abrasions and bruises are formed from the parts of the left front door. Question: what other sign confirms this? For example, pedal impressions on the sole of the footwear or fractures of the bones of the left leg.

t: Motorcycle trauma: kinds and seasonality
n: Motorcycle trauma: kinds and seasonality. In forensic practice, motorcycle trauma is much less frequent than automobile trauma. Seasonality is characteristic: it is observed mainly in late spring, summer and early autumn. A motorcycle is unstable, so the driver and passenger may be injured in all cases. There are 5 kinds of motorcycle trauma: collision with a pedestrian, running over by a wheel, falling from the motorcycle, striking another object, and combined trauma.

t: Motorcycle trauma and automobile trauma: comparison
n: Let us compare motorcycle trauma and automobile trauma. When a motorcycle collides with a pedestrian, the blow is delivered by the wheel, handlebar, lever and footrest. In the pedestrian, on the legs, pelvis and abdomen there are abrasions, bruises, contused-lacerated wounds; after the fall, craniocerebral injury. In a passenger in the sidecar, the ankle and knee joints are injured. In automobile trauma, the driver and passenger are not injured in all cases, there is a phase of sliding on the ground, bumper injuries occur on the legs, and running over by a wheel is more severe. In motorcycle trauma the driver and passenger are injured, there is no phase of sliding on the ground, there is an arc-shaped abrasion on the lower leg and thigh, and because the mass is small the injury is milder.

t: Rail trauma: kinds and structure of wheel and rail
n: Rail trauma: kinds and structure of wheel and rail. Rail trauma is the totality of injuries from moving railway transport, that is, a locomotive, electric locomotive and carriage; trams and rail-borne devices may also be included. There are six kinds: collision, running over by a wheel, fall, injury inside the transport, compression and combined trauma. The width of the rail head is 7–7.5 cm, and the width of the flange, that is, the reborda, on the inner side of the wheel facing the space between the rails, is 2.8–3.0 cm. If the body is caught between wheel and rail, a force of 5 tonnes or more acts per 1 square cm; the region is crushed, and the flange divides the body like scissors.

t: Rail trauma: T-shaped abrasion and compression band
n: Rail trauma: T-shaped abrasion and compression band. Skin pinched between the wheel flange and the rail head forms a T-shaped abrasion, also called the "pinch" sign. The T-shaped abrasion is on the side of the body facing the wheel, on the side of the space between the rails, in the region where the wheel leaves. Attention: the compression band is an even abrasion; the abrasion band is located at the edge, uneven, with scratches. The compression band is 12–14 cm on the wheel side and 7–8 cm on the rail side; it is soft, whitish, then dark brown. The abrasion band is 2–15 cm, wider and uneven on the wheel side. With the wheel of a light carriage, the band on the skin is 2–4 cm and is formed by the wheel flange alone.

t: Rail trauma: division of the body and trace substances
n: Rail trauma: division of the body and trace substances. When the body is divided, the compression band on the wheel side is also divided into two: the thin part, 2–3 cm, between the rails, and the wide part, 5–10 cm, outside the rail. On the rail side the edges of the division are relatively even. Outside the rail, from angular skin flaps, the edges are coarsely toothed; the angles point in the direction of movement. The edge of the bone fracture outside the rail is even, between the rails curved, with small fragments. Because of crushed tissues, a wedge-shaped defect is formed. Traces of oil, ballast substances and coal particles on clothing and the body are characteristic of rail trauma.

t: Case analysis: rail trauma
n: Case analysis: rail trauma. Situation: the body is divided into two parts, and there are traces of oil and coal particles on the clothing and skin. Question: which signs point to rail trauma? Traces of oil, ballast and coal are characteristic of this kind of trauma. Reason for the division: between the wheel and the rail the tissues are crushed, and the scissor-like action of the wheel flange separates them. Additional examination: the edge on the rail side should be even, and on the wheel side there should be angular toothed flaps.

t: Tractor trauma: wheeled and tracked
n: Tractor trauma: wheeled and tracked. Tractor trauma is rare, mainly in rural areas; its six kinds are similar to automobile trauma. In a tracked tractor, the teeth of the chain catch the clothing and body and draw it under the tractor. Because of the high specific action of the chain teeth, serious injuries are formed. The phases are similar to automobile trauma, but in a collision there is no 4th phase, and in running over no 2nd phase. In a wheeled tractor, the tread mark differs from that of an automobile; with a tracked one, a muddy mark corresponding to the track links remains on the clothing. The injury depends on the mass and the size of the wheel: abrasions, bruises and lacerated wounds occur.

t: Aviation trauma: kinds and damaging factors
n: Aviation trauma: kinds and damaging factors. Aviation trauma is divided into four kinds: injury inside the craft in flight, injury on leaving the craft in flight, injury on striking the ground, and injury from the craft on the ground. Causes: technical fault, meteorological factors, and violation of the rules of operation and servicing. Eight factors are counted: force, air stream, decompression, blunt objects, blast wave, thermal factor and external parts. Aviation trauma is an emergency event and is investigated by specialists; identification of bodies is important.

t: Action of aviation trauma factors
n: Action of aviation trauma factors. The blast wave destroys the craft and bodies; in an explosion on the ground, fragments are scattered within a radius of up to 500 m. The thermal factor gives burns in a fire; since the fuel tanks are located in the middle, they are more frequent in passengers. Toxic action: poisoning with carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, vinyl chloride and engine gases resulting from combustion. According to the table, dynamic force disturbs the blood supply of the brain, and loss of consciousness and displacement of internal organs are observed. At an air stream speed of 800 km/h and above, rupture of the mouth and barotrauma of the eyes and lungs occur. In decompression, rupture of the eardrum and gas bubbles appear.

t: Aviation trauma: two kinds of decompression
n: Aviation trauma: two kinds of decompression. At high altitude, that is, above 8 km, if the sealing of the cabin is breached, explosive decompression is observed. In it barotrauma of the lungs and of the ear, throat and nose occurs; usually the craft crashes, and the crew and passengers perish. On the body, the temporal bones are examined: rupture of the eardrum and haemorrhage in the middle and inner ear indicate loss of sealing. In flight at 19 km and above without protective equipment, altitude decompression, that is, emphysema, occurs: gas bubbles appear in the subcutaneous fat layer and in the vessels.

t: Aviation trauma: figures
n: Figures on aviation trauma. If the air stream speed is 800 km/h and above, it acts like a solid body: the corners of the mouth are torn, and the eyeball is damaged. Explosive decompression is observed in flight above 8 km, and altitude emphysema above 19 km. If an explosion occurs on the ground, small fragments of the body are scattered within a radius of up to 500 metres. For persons behind a turbojet engine, the jet of gas heated to 500–600 degrees causes mechanical and thermal injury. When the craft crashes, the force acting on the body may be several hundred, even a thousand times greater than in other transport trauma.

t: Aviation trauma: pilot's injuries and belt marks
n: Aviation trauma: pilot's injuries and belt marks. The pilot has particular injuries: the head striking the panel, the palm of the hand being crushed between the control column and the panel, the sole of the foot striking the pedals. On the sole of the pilot's footwear impressions of the pedal, and on the gloves impressions of the relief of the control column, may be found. Under the action of the safety belt there are an arc-shaped abrasion and bruise on the abdomen and chest and a transverse rupture of the abdominal wall. With a strong blow, complete separation of the upper part of the body by the belt is also possible.

t: Injuries from external parts of an aircraft
n: Injuries from external parts of an aircraft. Injuries may be received from the leading edge of the wings, propeller blades, the turbojet engine and the landing gear wheels. The leading edge of a wing gives persons on the runway a severe injury of the upper part of the body and amputation of the head and arm. Propeller blades produce multiple injuries of the head, arms and upper body, resembling chop wounds. In the turbojet engine a gas stream of 500–600 °C gives mechanical and thermal injury. Injuries from running over by the landing gear wheels resemble injury from the wheels of a heavy lorry.

t: Case analysis and quick question: aviation trauma
n: Case analysis and quick question: aviation trauma. Situation: in the cabin of an aircraft flying above 8 km, the sealing has been breached, the aircraft crashed, and the crew and passengers perished. The temporal bones are examined: rupture of the eardrum and haemorrhage in the middle and inner ear indicate loss of sealing. Attention! Explosive decompression, that is, 8 km and above with loss of sealing, is not altitude decompression; altitude decompression at 19 km and above is manifested by gas bubbles in flight without protection. Quick question: why is identification of the crew's bodies important? In the pilot, the state of health and toxic substances are also examined.

t: Conclusion: transport trauma and the physician's tasks
n: Conclusion: transport trauma and the physician's tasks. Transport trauma is the totality of injuries received from parts of a moving vehicle and from falling from it. More than 90% of examinations concern automobile trauma. Automobile trauma has 6 kinds. In a collision with a pedestrian 4 phases are distinguished, and in running over by a wheel 5 phases. The phase helps to determine the mechanism of injury. In motorcycle trauma 5 kinds are distinguished, in rail and tractor trauma 6 kinds, and in aviation trauma 4 kinds. In each, the injury depends on the structure of the part of the transport. The physician fully describes the injuries. He carefully removes the clothing and footwear, dries them, wraps them in paper and hands them to law enforcement authorities.
